title: Cure-SFT: Diagnostic-Guided Data Curation for Instruction Tuning
one_liner: Pick and fix the right training data instead of using all of it, and the model learns better with just ten percent.
lead: When you teach a language model to follow instructions, you feed it thousands of examples of instruction-answer pairs. But most datasets are bloated: they have copies of the same idea, examples with mistakes, and data that teaches nothing new. Cure-SFT is a method that picks the 10% of examples that matter most, fixes the broken ones, and ditches the rest — so your model learns better and faster, because each remaining example provides a clear, non-repetitive signal to learn from.

paras: Today's language models are taught via instruction tuning: you feed the model millions of (instruction, answer) pairs and it learns to follow the pattern. But in practice, datasets are a mess. Many examples teach the same thing — 'write a poem about winter' repeated 500 ways. Some examples are broken: wrong answers, garbled text, or instructions that make no sense. A naive approach throws everything at the model and hopes it learns, but that wastes compute and confuses the learner.

A beginner might try to fix this by randomly deleting examples to shrink the dataset. That doesn't work because you lose both good and bad data equally. Or they might score examples on quality alone and discard low-scorers — but that misses the core issue: redundancy and defects are different problems that need different fixes.

callout.html: Find duplicate-ish examples and remove them, find broken examples and fix them, then train on what's left.

panels.title: 1. The bloated dataset
panels.caption: Dataset has copies (free), broken examples (free), and a few good ones (hot).

panels.title: 2. Semantic redundancy: spot clusters

panels.caption: Group examples by meaning: many say similar things in different words.

panels.title: 3. Stratified sampling: pick from each cluster
panels.caption: Keep one good example per cluster, discard redundant copies.

panels.title: 4. Defect triage: fix or drop
panels.viz_args: Teacher model: this broken, this fixable, this beyond repair.
panels.caption: A teacher model grades each remaining example for fixability.

panels.title: 5. The lean, clean dataset
panels.caption: 10% remains: no copies, few defects, strong signal for learning.

steps.text: Map each example into a high-dimensional space and cluster: find groups of semantically similar instructions.
From each cluster, pick one representative example; discard the semantic duplicates.
A trained teacher model scores each remaining example on quality and fixability.
For examples rated as fixable, use the teacher to rewrite the broken parts (e.g., correct wrong answers).

steps.b: Step 5: Train on the curated set
steps.text: Train the student model on only the surviving, cleaned examples.

paras: Cure-SFT changes the dataset itself: it removes redundant examples and fixes defective ones before training begins. The model's structure stays the same; only the training data is curated and repaired.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: data redundancy score
hidden.name: semantic redundancy
paras: Every instruction in the dataset has a hidden redundancy score: how much of this example's meaning is already covered by other examples in the set. If ten examples say 'write a poem about winter' in different words, the ninth and tenth have high redundancy — they teach the model nothing new, just repetition. The method estimates this by embedding each example (converting it into a list of numbers capturing its meaning) and finding clusters. Examples in the center of a dense cluster are redundant; examples on the edge are unique.

The paper measures redundancy geometrically: how close is this example to its nearest neighbors in the embedding space. Close neighbors mean similar meaning, so close examples are redundant. The method keeps one example per cluster and discards the rest.

heat.caption: Darker means more redundant (close to other examples). Highlight marks are highly redundant, prime for removal.

reads.html: Redundancy is overlap: if example A and example B teach the same lesson, one is redundant.
The method uses stratified sampling in the embedding space: partition examples into clusters by nearest-neighbor distance, then keep one per cluster.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the two-phase fix
paras: Cure-SFT works because it separates two distinct problems. Redundancy and defects require opposite treatments: redundancy demands deletion (keep one copy, discard the rest), while defects demand repair (fix the answer, keep it). A method that treats both as 'low quality' will delete fixable examples and might keep unfixable trash, because both look like low-quality data.

The mechanism: first, remove redundancy via stratified sampling. By clustering examples in meaning-space and keeping one per cluster, the method ensures every remaining example teaches something new. This instantly shrinks the dataset and removes noise from repetition. Then, grade each survivor for fixability: a teacher model judges whether the defect is real but repairable (wrong answer + correct format) or inherent (malformed text, nonsense instruction). For fixable examples, rewrite the broken parts; for inherent defects, discard. The result is a lean, non-redundant, low-defect dataset. When the student model trains on this curated set, it receives clearer signals: every example is new, defects are fixed, and there is no noise from repetition.

stages.s: keep one per cluster, discard duplicates

math.words: for each cluster of nearby examples, keep one and discard the rest; the kept example is the one closest to the cluster center
math.equation: S_curated = select(C_i, argmin_j || x_j - mu_i ||) for all clusters i, where x_j in C_i
symbols: cluster i of semantically similar examples
the embedding (meaning vector) of example j
the center point of cluster i
the distance from example j to the cluster center

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Cluster 1: three examples about winter poetry. Embeddings (simplified): example A = [0.8, 0.2], example B = [0.81, 0.19], example C = [0.3, 0.7]. Cluster center = [0.60, 0.37].
A is closest, so keep A; discard B and C. Result: one strong example per cluster, no redundant copies.

math.note: The clustering is based on meaning-vectors (embeddings) rather than exact text match, so it catches paraphrases and variants that random deletion would miss.

charts.title: Baseline (all data)
charts.note: Training on full dataset: models learn but slowly, with confused update signals from redundant and broken examples.

charts.title: Cure-SFT (10% curated)
charts.note: Training on curated 10%: same or better performance with one-tenth the data and one-tenth the compute, because every example teaches something new and defects are fixed, so the model learns faster from a clearer signal.

items.html: If clusters are too coarse, the method discards legitimately different examples and the model underfits. The fix: tune the cluster granularity (sensitivity of the semantic grouping) on a held-out validation set.

items.b: Teacher model is biased or weak.
items.html: If the teacher model is poor at grading defects, it will mark fixable examples as irreparable and discard them. The method is only as good as the teacher. A better teacher (e.g., a larger model or human-annotated gold labels) improves results, because a more accurate grader filters correctly and preserves more high-quality examples.
When the teacher rewrites a defective example, it might hallucinate (invent incorrect details) if not careful. Verification by a second model or human spot-check is wise for high-stakes applications.

items.b: Done right: validation on held-out data.
items.html: Always evaluate the curated dataset on a separate validation set before training the student model, and compare against full-dataset baselines to ensure the savings are real.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show the two phases working: first, generate embeddings for 1000 instruction examples (use a pretrained embedding model like Sentence-BERT). Cluster them by cosine distance (pair-wise meaning similarity). Show that clustering removes 30-40% as semantic duplicates. Then, manually label 50 examples for quality: broken answer (defect), garbled text (defect), good (keep), or uncertain (fixable). Train a small scorer model on these 50 labels. Apply it to the remaining examples. Show that the scorer identifies defects with 70-80% accuracy on a held-out test set. Finally, train two models: one on all 1000 examples, one on the 600 curated examples. Compare accuracy on an instruction-following task. The curated model should reach the baseline in 1-2 epochs; the full model should need 3-4.
demo.closing: The demo makes undeniable: same or better accuracy, one-tenth the data, faster training. Redundancy removal and defect repair are real and measurable, because the curated model trains faster due to fewer examples and cleaner signals, and achieves higher accuracy because those remaining examples are all valuable.
